pages.text: STAGES OF CHANGE AND MOTIVATIONAL INTERVIEWING CHAPTER 11 1 | Understand the five stages of change. 2 | Describe the three aspects of motivation. 3 | Explain motivational interviewing and how it applies to nutrition coaching. 4 | Recognize strategies that make motivational interviewing more effective. LEARNING OBJECTIVES ISSA | Fitness Nutrition | 227

CHAPTER 11 | Stages of Change and Motivational Interviewing ISSA | Fitness Nutrition | 228 Making changes or adjustments to behaviors or lifestyle patterns can be a difficult task. Each individual will go through the process at their own pace and with their own setbacks and successes. The stages of change define the general steps for deciding to change, plan, and implement any type of behavior modification. Originally developed in the 1970s by James O. Prochaska and colleagues, the stages of change model is used to describe the thoughts, feelings, and behaviors of people in the process of change. The model outlines and clarifies the motivational conflicts people experience when making a change and is laid out to highlight the cyclical nature of the process. When interventions and therapies can be stage matched and are applicable to the stage of change a client is currently in, the interventions are typically more successful. These principles apply to psychological interventions as well as nutrition and dietary interventions in the health and wellness field. The motivations of an individual detail their reasons for behaving in a specific manner. The client’s intentions must be clearly defined and understood by both the client and the nutrition coach to ensure the program is appropriate. A process called motivational interviewing seeks to elicit behavior change while resolving ambivalence—having mixed feelings or contradictory ideas about something—for optimal results. THE STAGES OF CHANGE MODEL The stages of change model describes the stage of behavior change an individual is in at any given time and recognizes the following factors as necessary for behavior modification: 1 An increased awareness of the decision balance—the advantages (pros) of changing outweigh the disadvantages (cons) 2 Self-efficacy and autonomy—the ability to act independently to make choices 3 Strategies to make and maintain change—the avoidance of relapse STAGES OF CHANGE: The general steps for deciding to change, plan, and implement any type of behavior modification. STAGES OF CHANGE MODEL: The behavior change model used to describe the thoughts, feelings, and behaviors of people in the process of change. STAGE MATCHED: Interventions that are matched to the client’s current stage of change. AMBIVALENCE: Having mixed feelings or contradictory ideas about something or someone. RELAPSE: Falling back into previous behavior patterns.

ISSA | Fitness Nutrition | 229 DID YOU KNOW? The stages of change model describes 10 processes of change: 1 Consciousness raising - increasing awareness of the benefits of change and the risks of not changing 2 Dramatic relief - relief from aversive feelings about their behavior and feelings of hope when seeing other people in similar situations change 3 Self-reevaluation - the recognition that healthy behavior is an important part of who they are and want to be 4 Environmental reevaluation - the recognition that their unhealthy behavior has negative effects for others around them 5 Social liberation - feeling supported socially in making change 6 Self-liberation - feeling confident in one’s ability to change and be liberated from the negative effects of not changing 7 Helping relationships - feeling supported by others in changing 8 Counterconditioning - conditioning healthy behaviors and replacing unhealthy ones 9 Reinforcement management - associating positive rewards with healthy behaviors and reducing rewards from unhealthy behaviors 10 Stimulus control - learning to control environmental triggers to promote healthy behavior and reduce unhealthy behavior Figure 11.1 The Stages of Change. Pre-Contemplation There is no intention of addressing a behavior. Contemplation They are aware of the need to change but have barriers to overcome to address it. Maintenance They are continuing to do what is needed to maintain the desired behavior. Preparation They have the desire to change and are seeking a way. Action They are taking the necesssary steps to address their behavior and change it.

CHAPTER 11 | Stages of Change and Motivational Interviewing ISSA | Fitness Nutrition | 230 STAGE 1: PRE-CONTEMPLATION (NOT READY) People in this stage may not be consciously aware of the potential impacts of their current habits or they may not see a need to change right now. In some cases, they may not be aware that their habits are affecting their well-being. It is not uncommon for clients to say things like, “I feel fine with my current approach, but someone close to me encouraged me to talk with you,” or “I’m comfortable with my habits, but I’m open to learning more.” An important indicator of the pre-contemplation stage is that the perceived benefits of change don’t yet outweigh the perceived benefits of staying the same, and those in this stage may not feel a high sense of self-efficacy about making change. PRE-CONTEMPLATION There is no intention of addressing a behavior. To help them move toward change, the decisional balance can be explored in a way that helps the client consider new possibilities, while respecting their readiness. A coach can ask a client about their perception of their current habits and any impacts they’ve noticed on their daily life, energy, mood, or relationships through the use of questions such as these: • Describe how this habit affects your daily, weekly, and monthly life. Looking ahead, what do you think might happen if you keep things as they are? • If you think about your relationships, have you noticed any ways this habit influences others around you? • What’s your view of the change you’re considering, and what do you think it might add to your life? • Would you be interested in learning more about this habit and possible options for change? Change can be achieved only through a shift in a client’s perception that aligns with their own goals and values. To support this, a nutrition coach should ask their client to do the following: • Rate their confidence in their ability to change

ISSA | Fitness Nutrition | 231 • Identify what steps can be taken to raise their confidence • Name any barriers they experience • Define what aspects of change feel most challenging for them Coach’s Role: In this stage, focus on curiosity, respectful exploration, and sharing information only when invited. Avoid persuading or “selling” change; let the client lead the pace. STAGE 2: CONTEMPLATION (GETTING READY) When the decision balance is equal, a client sees the cons and pros of making a behavior change as about the same. This often causes a stalemate where change is postponed, there is a high degree of ambivalence, and self-efficacy has not yet fully developed. People at this stage will often say things like, “I know I would feel better if I made some nutrition changes, but I just don’t know if I can,” or “I know I might enjoy being more active, but I’m not sure I can fit it in.” CONTEMPLATION They are aware of the need to change but have barriers to overcome to address it. In the contemplation stage, the decisional balance is at a deadlock. Because ambivalence is normal here, it’s helpful to increase awareness of overlooked benefits of change and to highlight the client’s existing capabilities and past successes. A quick way to explore readiness in the contemplation stage is with scaling questions. For example: “On a scale of 1–10, how ready do you feel to make this change?” Follow up with, “What would help move you one point higher?” These questions help clients verbalize their motivation and barriers while giving you a snapshot of their current mindset. Possible Coach Questions: • In what ways might your relationships, energy, or daily routine improve if you made this change? • In what ways might your work life (or productivity) improve if you made this change? • How would you see yourself differently if you made this change?

CHAPTER 11 | Stages of Change and Motivational Interviewing ISSA | Fitness Nutrition | 232 Additionally, a nutrition coach can draw attention to other successes a client has had in the past and their ability to successfully make behavior modifications by asking questions like these: • Can you tell me about times you’ve made a change that you felt good about? • What other challenges have you overcome? • What strategies worked for you then? Coach’s Role: In this stage, help clients explore overlooked benefits of change and draw out their own reasons for action. Use open-ended and scaling questions to assess readiness, and reflect back their past successes to build confidence. Avoid pressuring them into decisions; instead, let insights surface naturally. STAGE 3: PREPARATION (READY) People in the preparation stage are ready to take action. They see the pros as greater than the cons, and they’ve begun planning small, manageable steps toward change. Here, people will often begin to plan and initiate small steps toward change; however, self-doubt may still be present, and self-efficacy is growing but not yet solid. Clients in the preparation stage will say things like, “I’m going to start bringing lunch to work three days a week, but I’m still figuring out how to prep ahead,” or “I’m planning to move more in my day, but I’m not sure how to keep it going when work gets busy.” In the preparation stage, scaling questions can help strengthen commitment and surface lingering doubts. You might ask, “On a scale of 1–10, how confident are you that you can follow through with your plan?” and, “What support would help raise that number?” The coach’s role is to strengthen confidence and normalize setbacks as part of learning. Questions to reframe failure: • What’s your attitude toward setbacks? • What have you learned from challenges in the past? • If something doesn’t work once, what could help you try again? PREPARATION They have the desire to change and are seeking a way.

ISSA | Fitness Nutrition | 233 Encouraging clients to identify supporters, plan for high-risk situations, and set up accountability systems can help maintain momentum before action begins. Coach’s Role: Here, focus on strengthening self-efficacy and planning practical first steps. Normalize setbacks as part of the process, and encourage clients to anticipate high-risk situations. Use scaling questions to identify confidence levels and address barriers before action begins. STAGE 4: ACTION In the action stage, the client is actively taking measurable steps toward their goal through conscious effort. This stage can last up to six months. In this stage, clients might say, “I’ve been preparing my meals ahead for the past month, and it’s helping me feel more energized,” or “I’ve kept up with my walking routine, and I’m sleeping better.” While confidence is growing, the novelty of new behaviors can fade. Commitment strategies such as pairing new habits with enjoyable ones, removing unnecessary barriers, and tracking progress can help sustain motivation. Useful questions: • What benefits have you noticed since making this change? • What strategies are helping you stay consistent? • What deeper reason keeps you motivated to continue? Coach’s Role: Support clients in maintaining momentum by reinforcing commitment strategies and celebrating progress. Help them troubleshoot challenges as they arise, and connect daily actions to deeper motivations. Encourage habit tracking and social support to make the new behavior stick. ACTION They are taking the necessary steps to address their behavior and change it.

CHAPTER 11 | Stages of Change and Motivational Interviewing ISSA | Fitness Nutrition | 234 STAGE 5: MAINTENANCE In the maintenance stage, clients have sustained their changes for more than six months. Confidence and consistency are higher, and the pros of change clearly outweigh the cons. While behaviors feel more automatic, stressful situations or major life changes can still challenge new habits. Clients may say, “I’ve been feeling really good with my current routine, but I’m wondering how to keep it going during the holidays,” or “I’ve been consistent with movement and meal planning, but I want to make sure I don’t slip back during busy work weeks.” Coaches can support maintenance by helping clients: • Identify stress triggers and coping strategies. • Maintain or deepen their social support network. • Explore new challenges or goals to keep growth engaging. Coach’s Role: In this stage, focus on sustaining gains, reinforcing identity as a person who maintains healthy behaviors, and preventing relapse. Help clients identify stress triggers, expand coping strategies, and set new goals to keep growth engaging. Keep the conversation focused on autonomy, mastery, and purpose to maintain long-term motivation. MAINTENANCE They are continuing to do what is needed to maintain the desired behavior. DETERMINING MOTIVATION The language clients use to answer questions can provide valuable insight into their motivation. Listening for both what is said and how it is said can help a coach understand the client’s current stage of change and their personal priorities. Open-ended questions are key in expanding the conversation about what truly matters to them and help them reflect on their own reasons for change. This type of question requires more than a yes or no answer and forces the client to probe deeper. A coach can also use the following more specific questions to assess the stage of change and discover motivation: OPEN-ENDED QUESTIONS: Probing questions that require more than a yes or no response.

ISSA | Fitness Nutrition | 235 • What’s most important to you about making this change? • What do you see as the main benefits for you? • What might be some challenges you’ll want to plan for? • On a scale of 1–10, how confident do you feel about following through—1 meaning “not at all” and 10 meaning “I’m fully confident”? • On a scale of 1–10, how strong are the factors that may derail your plans—1 meaning “they will not affect me” and 10 meaning “I cannot control my reaction to these factors”? THE ELEMENTS OF MOTIVATION Motivation, the reason people behave the way they do, is composed of three key elements: autonomy, mastery, and purpose. Within the stages of change, each element of motivation is important and must be achieved to reach maintenance. A nutrition coach should understand each of these elements to successfully progress clients through the stages of changing their behavior within a coaching program for the following reasons: • When people are given the autonomy and have confidence, motivation increases. • When people can achieve mastery over what they are doing, motivation increases. • When people have a deeper sense of purpose for the things they do, they are much more motivated to do them. AUTONOMY Autonomy refers to the ability to make your own choices and take actions that align with your values. In coaching, supporting autonomy means the client feels ownership of their process rather than being told what to do. Autonomy versus Motivation When autonomy increases, so does motivation. Clients are more engaged when they can decide what to focus on, when to take action, and how to do it in a way that works for them.

CHAPTER 11 | Stages of Change and Motivational Interviewing ISSA | Fitness Nutrition | 236 Table 11.1 Autonomy and Motivation Spectrum. High Autonomy and Motivation Low Autonomy and Motivation Choosing foods they enjoy Following a restrictive diet Setting personal nutrition goals Goals decided entirely by someone else Deciding meal timing based on preference Eating at prescribed times regardless of hunger Adjusting portions based on hunger cues Eating predetermined portions regardless of satiety MASTERY Mastery describes the state of having competence that comes from learning and improving over time. It’s not about perfection, but about growing skills, building confidence, and recognizing progress. When people feel capable, their motivation strengthens. Even small wins, like learning a new recipe or completing a workout they once found challenging, can reinforce their belief in their ability to sustain change. Mastery versus Motivation Like autonomy, mastery exists on a sliding scale and is constantly changing. The relationship of mastery to education also means that clients and coaches must continue to learn and keep up with changes and research that may affect their present knowledge levels. As mastery levels decrease, research has shown a deleterious effect on motivation levels. Coaches can help by: • Celebrating progress, no matter how small. • Offering skill-building opportunities that match the client’s stage. • Encouraging reflection on what they’ve learned so far.

ISSA | Fitness Nutrition | 237 Table 11.2 Mastery and Motivation High Mastery & Motivation Low Mastery & Motivation Preparing a favorite healthy meal they’ve made many times Feeling pressured to follow an unfamiliar meal plan Confidently choosing foods that align with their nutrition goals Unsure how to choose foods that meet their needs Knowing exactly how to follow a recipe or prep routine Unclear about how to prepare or cook healthy meals PURPOSE Purpose is the deeper “why” behind a client’s actions. It connects daily habits to personal values and long-term vision. When clients know why a change matters to them, beyond surface goals, they are more likely to stay committed. Purpose evolves as clients grow. For some, it may start as wanting more energy to play with their kids; for others, it may become about aging well, improving quality of life, or feeling confident in their own choices. Coaches can explore purpose with questions like: • What will this change make possible for you? • How does this goal fit into the life you want to live? • When you picture your future, how does this change support that vision?

CHAPTER 11 | Stages of Change and Motivational Interviewing ISSA | Fitness Nutrition | 238 Table 11.3 Purpose and Motivation. High Purpose & Motivation Low Purpose & Motivation Eating to support long-term health and energy for meaningful life goals Eating without a clear sense of why it matters for their health or life Staying committed to nutrition changes because they align with personal values Making changes only because of outside pressure, not personal meaning Feeling inspired to try new foods that support well-being Lacking interest in exploring healthier options BUILDING HABITS FOR SUSTAINABLE CHANGE Motivation sparks the desire to act, but habits keep the change going over the long term. Helping clients understand how habits form can make healthy actions feel easier and more automatic over time. The Habit Loop Habits are built through a loop of three components: • Cue: a trigger that starts the behavior • Routine: the action itself • Reward: a positive outcome or feeling that reinforces the behavior For example, if the cue is finishing work for the day, the routine might be preparing a healthy dinner, and the reward might be feeling satisfied and energized afterward. Practical Habit Strategies for Nutrition Coaching • Habit stacking: Pair a new habit with an existing one. Example: After making your morning coffee (existing habit), prepare your daily snack portions (new habit). • Micro-habits: Break a goal into small, easy steps. Example: Instead of committing to cooking every meal at home, begin with preparing one healthy lunch per week. • Environmental design: Make the desired behavior easier and the undesired behavior harder. Example: Keep pre-chopped vegetables at eye level in the fridge and store sugary snacks out of immediate reach. HABIT STACKING: Linking a new habit to an existing one so the established behavior acts as a trigger for the new action MICRO-HABITS: Very small, simple actions that are easy to start and sustain, helping build momentum for larger behavior changes ENVIRONMENTAL DESIGN: Structuring one’s surroundings to make desired behaviors easier to do and undesired behaviors harder to do.

ISSA | Fitness Nutrition | 239 MOTIVATIONAL INTERVIEWING The motivational interviewing (MI) model is a widely accepted approach to elicit behavior change. Developed by clinical psychologists William R. Miller and Stephen Rollnick, MI works by strengthening the client’s own motivation and commitment rather than trying to convince them to change. It places the power to make modifications in the hands of the client and improves autonomy and confidence while seeking to resolve any ambivalence or indecision that may stall success. The premise of MI is that that people are more likely to change when they feel respected, understood, and empowered to choose their own path. MI as a behavioral change method is based upon the following assumptions: • All people possess the capacity for growth and change. • The power to change is within the client. • Ambivalence is a normal part of change that becomes a motivational obstacle in the process of change. • Ambivalence can be overcome through the coach-client alliance as a collaborative partnership that incorporates the expertise of both parties. MI is guided by five unique principles: 1 Express empathy through reflective listening. 2 Explore and work with ambivalence instead of pushing past it. 3 Avoid argument or direct confrontation. 4 Adjust to resistance rather than meeting it head-on. 5 Support autonomy, optimism, and self-efficacy. DEEPENING MOTIVATIONAL INTERVIEWING PRACTICE Motivational interviewing (MI) is most effective when its core skills are applied consistently. The OARS model offers a simple way to remember and practice these skills.

CHAPTER 11 | Stages of Change and Motivational Interviewing ISSA | Fitness Nutrition | 240 TABLE 11.4 OARS SKILLS OVERVIEW OARS Skill What It Means Example Coach Prompt Open questions Invite detailed responses and exploration What changes would you most like to see in your eating habits? Affirmations Recognize and reinforce client strengths You’ve shown real consistency in preparing meals at home. Reflective Listening Restate or rephrase to confirm understanding You feel more energized when you have a balanced breakfast. Summarizing Pull together key points to maintain focus So far, you’ve said you want more energy, you feel better when you prep lunches, and you’d like quick dinner ideas. RECOGNIZING CHANGE TALK VS. SUSTAIN TALK In MI, the way a client talks about change offers important clues about their readiness and motivation. • Change talk are statements a client makes that show desire, ability, reason, or need to make a change. • Sustain talk are statements a client makes that support keeping things the same or maintaining their current behavior. The goal is to encourage more change talk while acknowledging sustain talk without judgment. This keeps the conversation supportive and forward-looking. Examples: • Change Talk: “I’ve noticed I feel more focused when I eat lunch, so I’d like to make it a daily habit.” • Sustain Talk: “I know skipping lunch isn’t ideal, but it’s the only way I get everything done.” CHANGE TALK: Client statements that express desire, ability, reasons, or commitment to make a positive behavior change. SUSTAIN TALK: Client statements that express desire, reasons, or commitment to maintain current behaviors or resist change.

ISSA | Fitness Nutrition | 241 EXPRESS EMPATHY Empathy in motivational interviewing is an intentional skill. It means understanding the client’s perspective and feelings and reflecting that understanding back in a way that shows respect and acceptance. This helps create a safe, collaborative space where clients feel heard and supported. An empathic style does the following: • Shows respect and acceptance for the client’s experiences and feelings (for example, “I hear what you’re saying” or “We’re a team, and we’ll work through this together”). • Acknowledges effort without judgment, offering encouragement like, “Look at how far you’ve come and the steps you’re taking.” • Listens more than you talk, ensuring the conversation is guided by the client’s perspective. • Persuades gently, offering suggestions only in alignment with the client’s goals (“You mentioned your energy has improved since adding a snack. What do you think about adding one later in the day too?”). • Provides consistent support throughout the coaching process (“You’re making steady progress, and I’m here to help with any challenges that come up”). • The client wants to feel that whenever they are with the coach, they will be in a safe, open, and nonjudgmental environment. They want to feel assured that the coach will understand their unique perspective, feelings, and values. MI is most successful when a trusting relationship is established between client and coach. The key is to listen.

CHAPTER 11 | Stages of Change and Motivational Interviewing ISSA | Fitness Nutrition | 242 DID YOU KNOW? There are 12 barriers to effective listening. 1 Ordering or directing. Directing someone involves assuming the role of authority or power in the relationship. The coach may be the one a client views who is in a position of power, or the words may simply be phrased and spoken in an authoritarian manner. 2 Warning or threatening. Threats and warnings are similar to ordering but include an overt or covert threat of impending negative consequences if the advice or direction is not followed. The threat may be one the nutrition coach will carry out or simply a prediction of a negative outcome if the client doesn’t comply—for example, “If you don’t listen to me and do what I’m telling you, you’ll be sorry.” 3 Giving advice, making suggestions, or providing solutions prematurely or when unsolicited. The message recommends a course of action based on the nutrition coach’s knowledge and personal experience. These recommendations often begin with phrases such as, “What I would do is…” 4 Persuading with logic, arguing, or lecturing. Persuading, and especially lecturing, implies that the client is either not capable or has not reasoned through the problem adequately and needs help to do so. 5 Moralizing, preaching, or telling clients their duty. Moral statements, like ordering, assume a position of authority or dominance and often contain such words as “should” or “ought” to convey moral instructions. 6 Judging, criticizing, disagreeing, or blaming. Blaming and criticizing almost always shut down communication as they imply that something is wrong with the client or with what the client has said. Even simple disagreement may be interpreted as criticizing.

ISSA | Fitness Nutrition | 243 12 barriers to effective listening (Continued) 7 Agreeing, approving, or praising. When whatever the client has said is agreed with, the underlying message is that what the client does has no relevance— as everything is always approved. Unsolicited approval can also interrupt the communication process (sometimes clients feel that they are not listened to) and can imply an uneven relationship between the nutrition coach speaking and the client who is listening. Reflective listening does not require agreement. 8 Shaming, ridiculing, labeling, or name-calling. Shaming and ridiculing are forms of contempt and express overt disapproval and intent to correct a specific behavior or attitude. There is perhaps no greater barrier to communication and listening than shaming. 9 Interpreting or analyzing. Nutrition coaches can be frequently and easily tempted to impose their own interpretations on a client’s statement and to find some hidden, analytical meaning. Interpretive statements might imply that the nutrition coach knows more about the client’s real problem than the client does. 10 Reassuring, sympathizing, or consoling. Nutrition coaches often want to make the client feel better by offering consolation. Such reassurance can interrupt the flow of communication and interfere with careful listening. 11 Questioning or probing. Nutrition coaches often mistake questioning for good listening. Although the nutrition coach may ask questions to learn more about the client, the underlying message is that the nutrition coach might find the right answer to all the client’s problems if enough questions are asked. In fact, intensive questioning can interfere with the spontaneous flow of communication and divert it in directions of interest to the nutrition coach rather than the client. 12 Withdrawing, distracting, humoring, or changing the subject. Although humor may represent an attempt to take the client’s mind off the barriers and obstacles to that client making changes in their life, it also can be a distraction that diverts communication and implies that the client’s statements are unimportant.

CHAPTER 11 | Stages of Change and Motivational Interviewing ISSA | Fitness Nutrition | 244 UNCOVER AMBIVALENCE In uncovering ambivalence, the goal is to create a discrepancy between what a person is currently doing (their current nutrition, lifestyle, and activity patterns) and where they would like to be (their vision for health, energy, or quality of life). When this gap becomes visible, clients can better see what is at stake and may become more open to exploring change. Ambivalence is an expected part of the change process. It is the inner tug-of-war between wanting things to be different and wanting things to stay the same. This can show up as hesitation, delay, or starting and stopping repeatedly. Recognizing and working with ambivalence, rather than pushing against it, helps the client feel heard and supported. Listening carefully when clients talk about what matters most to them allows the coach to: • Identify values and priorities that can guide change. • Hear past experiences with change that shape current beliefs. • Understand barriers or fears that may be slowing progress. Ambivalence might look like the client who talks enthusiastically in a session about wanting more energy and better health but later feels uncertain, overwhelmed, or pulled back into old routines. For change to last, the coach must help the client explore and name the source of this ambivalence, using reflective statements and open-ended questions to deepen self- awareness. This approach builds trust, strengthens the coaching alliance, and helps the client uncover their own reasons and readiness for change, which is far more powerful than being told what to do. AVOID ARGUMENT In MI, the goal is to have the client voice reasons for change, not to be convinced by the coach. Trying to prove a point often triggers defensiveness or a power struggle. Instead, stay curious, reflective, and non-confrontational. For example: • Instead of: “You need to stop drinking soda.” • Try: “You’ve said you’d like more energy during the day. What role do you think your beverage choices might play in that?” This keeps the focus on the client’s own reasoning and autonomy.

ISSA | Fitness Nutrition | 245 RESISTANCE IS A SIGNAL Client resistance is a normal and expected part of the change process. Every client will face moments where progress feels harder, and overcoming those moments often takes time, patience, and ongoing support. Resistance can appear in many ways. Clients can show resistance by behaving defiantly or, conversely, by showing a lack of effort toward the changes they have declared they wish to make. Rather than viewing resistance as a setback, nutrition coaches can see it as valuable feedback. It is often a signal that the current approach, pace, or focus may not be fully aligned with the client’s needs, values, or readiness. In this way, resistance becomes an invitation to pause, listen more closely, and adjust the conversation. Hidden in every struggle is an opportunity to respond in a new and possibly more effective way. Adjusting to resistance is much like avoiding an argument: it keeps the dialogue collaborative, honors client autonomy, and reinforces that the coaching relationship is a partnership. By meeting clients where they are, the coach helps maintain trust and keeps progress moving forward, even when the pace changes. Here are seven strategies to help a nutrition coach navigate client resistance: 1 Simple Reflection The simplest way to respond to resistance is to repeat the client’s statement in a neutral tone. This shows you have heard them, affirms their perspective, and can invite them to share more or even voice the opposite viewpoint. Client: I don’t plan to change what I’m doing anytime soon. Nutrition coach: Right now, you don’t see much reason to change your eating or activity habits. 2 Amplified Reflection This approach restates the client’s statement in a slightly more extreme form, without sarcasm. By gently magnifying their words, you may prompt the client to soften their position and consider a different perspective. Client: I don’t know why my family is worried about my eating habits. Nutrition coach: From your point of view, their concern has no real basis at all. 3 Double-Sided Reflection This skill reflects both sides of the client’s own statements, starting with their reasons for not changing (sustain talk) and ending with their reasons for change

CHAPTER 11 | Stages of Change and Motivational Interviewing ISSA | Fitness Nutrition | 246 (change talk). It acknowledges ambivalence while guiding the conversation toward their motivation. Client: My partner wants me to stop drinking soda, but I’m not going to quit completely. Nutrition coach: You don’t want to give it up entirely, and you’ve also said that cutting back could help you feel more energized during the day. 4 Shifting Focus This technique redirects the conversation away from a roadblock and toward a topic the client feels more open to exploring. It reduces tension while honoring the client’s autonomy in choosing what to address. Client: I can’t stop eating fried food when I’m out with friends. Nutrition coach: Being with friends makes that a challenge right now. What other changes to your eating or activity feel more doable at the moment? 5 Agreement with a Twist This skill begins with genuine agreement to validate the client’s perspective, then adds a small redirection that opens the door to exploring new possibilities without dismissing their concerns. Client: Why is everyone so focused on what I eat? I feel fine, and I wish people would just stop talking about it. Nutrition coach: I hear you; those kinds of comments can undermine your confidence and make it harder to focus on what matters to you. I also hear that feeling well is important to you, and we can work on ways to support that in a way that feels comfortable for you. 6 Reframing Reframing offers a new, more constructive interpretation of what the client has said. It helps shift how they view a situation, moving from a negative or limiting frame to one that aligns with their values or strengths. Client: My coworkers think it is strange that I eat every three hours instead of just at lunch and dinner. Nutrition coach: They may have a different routine, but for you, eating more regularly helps keep your energy steady and your focus sharp. 7 Siding with the Negative OThis strategy involves briefly taking the client’s stated position against change, which can lead them to argue the opposite and voice their own reasons for change. It should be used carefully and usually later in the conversation, once rapport is established. Client: I don’t think my eating habits are that bad.

ISSA | Fitness Nutrition | 247 Nutrition coach: Maybe there is no real need to change right now. What, if anything, would need to happen for you to see it differently? TABLE 11.5: RESISTANCE STRATEGIES QUICK REFERENCE Strategy Quick Definition Example Simple Reflection Repeat the client’s words neutrally to show you heard them. Client: I don’t plan to change. Amplified Reflection Restate in a slightly stronger way to prompt rethinking. Client: My family is worried about my eating. Coach: From your view, their concern has no real basis at all. Double-Sided Reflection Reflect both sides, ending with the reason for change. Client: I’m not quitting soda. Coach: You’re not ready to give it up, and you’ve said cutting back could boost your energy. Shifting Focus Move from a roadblock to something more doable. Client: I can’t stop eating fried food with friends. Coach: Being with friends makes that hard. What other changes feel doable? Agreement with a Twist Agree, then gently redirect to new possibilities. Client: Why is everyone so focused on what I eat? Coach: You’re right, constant comments can be discouraging. Feeling well matters to you, and we can work on ways to support that. Reframing Offer a more positive or constructive view. Client: Coworkers think it’s strange I eat every three hours. Coach: They may see it differently, but for you, it keeps your energy steady. Siding with the Negative Take their position to spark them to argue the opposite. Client: My eating isn’t that bad. Coach: Maybe there’s no need to change right now. What would need to happen for you to see it differently?

CHAPTER 11 | Stages of Change and Motivational Interviewing ISSA | Fitness Nutrition | 248 SUPPORT CLIENTS WITH OPTIMISM AND ENTHUSIASM Many clients do not believe they have the power to make lasting changes in their lives. However, the reality is that everyone possesses the capacity for change. By giving a client hope, optimism, and encouragement that they can change and that the coach will be there to help them every step of the way, the coach can help a client see that they have the power within them to make the changes they want and to reach their goals. Confidence is key for self-efficacy and can also drive motivation. Staying Within Scope of Practice A nutrition coach is responsible for providing guidance within their area of training and certification. This means avoiding activities such as diagnosing illnesses, prescribing medication, or giving medical treatment. Examples of Out-of-Scope Topics • Interpreting blood test results • Advising on prescription changes • Treating injuries or medical conditions Redirecting with Care: When clients ask questions outside your scope, respond with empathy and a helpful next step. • Example 1: “That is an important question for your doctor. In the meantime, we can focus on your meal planning so you are ready when you get more information.” • Example 2: “It sounds like you would like clarity on your lab results. Let us make sure you get that from your healthcare provider, and we can talk about how to support your goals once you have their recommendations.” MOTIVATIONAL INTERVIEWING STRATEGIES STRATEGY #1: ASK OPEN-ENDED QUESTIONS Open-ended questions encourage clients to explore their thoughts, feelings, and experiences in more depth. Unlike yes-or-no questions, they invite longer responses, uncover what truly matters to the client, and keep the conversation client-led. These questions help the coach: • Understand the client’s perspective without assumptions. • Gather information in a neutral way.

ISSA | Fitness Nutrition | 249 • Keep the client talking and engaged. • Prevent premature judgments by focusing on exploration rather than quick answers. Here are some examples: • How has your body changed since we started working together? • Which of the nutritional changes you’ve made do you like best and why? • Besides having more energy, strength, and tone, what other benefits have you noticed from eating better and being more active? When coaches use open-ended questions consistently, clients do more of the talking, take ownership of their insights, and often reveal motivations or challenges that might not surface otherwise. STRATEGY #2: LISTEN REFLECTIVELY Reflective listening means accurately hearing and understanding a client’s message, then restating it in your own words to confirm meaning. Instead of asking a new question, the coach responds with a statement that mirrors or paraphrases what the client has said. This checks understanding, prevents assumptions, and deepens the empathic connection between coach and client. Nutrition coach: What else concerns you about your exercise and eating habits? Client: Well, I’m not sure I’m concerned about it, but I do wonder sometimes if I’m not doing enough or eating too much. Nutrition coach: You’re noticing times when you might be eating more than feels right for you. Client: Yes, too much junk food for my own good, I guess. Sometimes when I wake up in the morning, I feel awful, and I feel awful for the rest of the day. Nutrition coach: Feeling that way makes you wonder if your food choices or activity levels are part of the reason. Client: Yes, and it makes me tired and lethargic. Nutrition coach: Tell me more about what you’ve noticed. Client: Well, I don’t get outside much during the week, and I usually grab quick meals that are not always the healthiest.

CHAPTER 11 | Stages of Change and Motivational Interviewing ISSA | Fitness Nutrition | 250 Nutrition coach: You’re seeing that less movement and quick meals might be affecting how you feel day to day. Client: Exactly, and I think I’d like to start changing that. Nutrition coach: Ok; you’re ready to make some adjustments to feel more energized and healthier overall.. STRATEGY #3: SUMMARIZE Summarizing means capturing the key points a client has shared and reflecting them back in a concise way. It reinforces that you have been listening, highlights important themes, and helps the client see the bigger picture. A well-timed summary can close one part of the conversation and smoothly transition to the next. It is especially useful at the beginning or end of a session, or when the client is moving between stages of change. The coach can choose what to emphasize, leave out less relevant details, and invite the client to add or clarify. This often prompts new insights and keeps the dialogue collaborative. STRATEGY #4: AFFIRM AND VALIDATE Affirming means recognizing and acknowledging a client’s strengths, efforts, or values. Validating means showing understanding and acceptance of their experiences and feelings. When done sincerely, both strengthen trust and rapport. By affirming, the coach communicates, “I see your effort, and I believe in your ability to change.” Reminding clients of past successes can help them tap into autonomy, increase confidence, and see themselves as capable of making and sustaining change. This can be especially valuable for preventing discouragement or relapse. STRATEGY #5: UNCOVERING AND ADDRESSING AMBIVALENCE Ambivalence is a normal part of the change process. It occurs when a client feels pulled in two directions. Part of them wants to make a change, and another part wants to keep things the same. This inner conflict can create hesitation, delay action, or lead to starting and stopping repeatedly. Recognizing and working with ambivalence, rather than pushing past it, is central to helping clients progress. Scaling questions are a practical way to bring ambivalence into the open. They ask clients to rate aspects of their motivation, readiness, or confidence on a numerical scale, which makes abstract feelings more concrete and easier to explore. SCALING QUESTIONS: Simple questions that ask for a response on a sliding scale—for example, 1 to 10.

ISSA | Fitness Nutrition | 251 Examples of desire or readiness questions: • On a scale of 1–10, how much do you want to improve your overall health? • On a scale of 1–10, how ready do you feel to make this change? Examples of confidence or barrier questions: • On a scale of 1–10, how confident are you that you can follow through on this change? • On a scale of 1–10, how likely is it that obstacles could stop you from reaching your goal Once the client responds, the coach can explore their number by asking: • What made you choose that number and not a lower one? (This draws out existing motivation.) • What would it take to move that number one point higher? (This identifies possible solutions.) If discrepancies between desire and confidence emerge, the coach can reflect them back: • It sounds like you really want this change, but you’re not sure you can maintain it right now. From there, the conversation can shift to identifying small, achievable steps that increase confidence and reduce the weight of uncertainty. The goal is to help the client voice their own reasons for change and name the resources or strategies they already have. When clients articulate their next steps themselves, they are far more likely to follow through. This not only builds ownership of the process, but it also strengthens their self- belief that they can succeed.
